newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil plays down fears of huge trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil plays down fears of huge trade gap.

text.p: Brazilian officials on Wednesday played down forecasts of a massive October trade gap, saying the deficit was not likely to exceed $500 million and the full-year gap should be close to 1995's $3.157 billion.

A senior government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the markets should concentrate instead on the current account deficit, which he predicted would total about 2.5 percent of gross domestic product for 1996.
He angrily dismissed a newspaper report that October could show a trade deficit as high as $1.5 billion, after September's $655 million gap.
The Central Bank's director of monetary policy, Francisco Lopes, said in an interview published on Wednesday that the markets' preoccupation with trade was "unnecessary."
"Brazil today has very comfortable (current account) numbers," Lopes told the Jornal do Brasil daily, adding, "In 1996, the trade deficit will be similar to 1995."
Brazilian Brady Bonds came under pressure on Tuesday after exports in October's third week fell to one of their lowest weekly levels this year, averaging just $168.8 million a day.
"You have to see the woods and not the trees," the senior government source said. Exports in October are expected to reach $4.0 billion and imports no more than $4.5 billion, he said.
Exports on October 22 totalled $190.6 million, while imports continued "steady," he said.
"We imagine the October trade deficit will be more like June ($327 million) or July ($334 million)," he said. The high September figure was an "accident" caused by high oil imports, he said.
The source said it was logical to predict a deficit for the remaining months of the year because exports of agricultural products, particularly soybeans, would slow to a trickle.
Exports of other goods, such as steel, will also drop because today's shipments are for January delivery, a seasonally low-demand month in foreign markets.
The source said Christmas sales were likely to raise purchases by some 5.0 percent.
The Central Bank's Lopes told Jornal do Brasil that it was not a concern that the full-year trade deficit might exceed original government predictions of "more-or-less equilibrium."
"It only shows the government was optimistic," he said.
Both the government source and Lopes said it was important to bear in mind that Brazil did not yet know what its "natural" trade balance should be following a few years of economic opening.
The source defended a change in the way the Central Bank calculates GDP for its external accounts, saying the previous method underestimated Brazil's GDP.
"We expect the current account gap to be about 2.5 percent (of GDP in 1996)," he said. "I see no justification for so much speculation about the trade balance."
